entries.clue: More opportune to stretch out during watch? (8)

indicatorNotes.during: What happens during something else happens inside it, so the short word goes within the longer one rather than beside it.

blocks.note: a watch is a timer, the thing that counts off the minutes
to stretch out on a sofa is to lie on it

annotation.surface: A sailor wondering whether the night watch is the better moment for a lie-down.
annotation.walkthrough: The watch on the surface is a spell of guard duty; the one the clue wants is the thing that ticks. Comparatives like this are awkward English but perfectly legal words.
annotation.definitionFit: Something timelier arrives at a better moment than the alternative, which is what calling an act more opportune says about it.

entries.clue: Result of my eye operation? You’ve explained it (1,3)

annotation.definitionNote: Neither half is a synonym for a word: the answer is a spoken sentence, and both halves describe the occasion on which somebody says it.

blocks.note: surgery gives the patient their sight back, so afterwards the two words are literally true of them
the stock two words you say when the penny drops and somebody's explanation has landed

annotation.surface: A patient just out of eye surgery, and someone else finally making something clear.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves are the same two spoken words, which is why the clue has no joinery at all. The question mark carries the first definition: what the operation produces is the sentence itself, not a condition with a name.
annotation.definitionFit: Eye surgery restores sight, so the words are literally true afterwards; the same two words are the stock reply once an explanation has landed.

entries.clue: Veto being lifted, rest seized (6)

indicatorNotes.being lifted: In a down clue something lifted is raised back up the grid, so its letters are read from the bottom to the top.

blocks.note: a veto is a BAN, here written upwards
a bed is where you rest

annotation.surface: A veto lifted, and whatever was left of the goods confiscated.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rest' is the trap: it offers the remainder and delivers the furniture. Lifting a ban is the surface's own news story, so the reversal instruction hides in plain sight.
annotation.definitionFit: To nab somebody is to grab or arrest them on the spot, the informal verb for seizing a person or a thing.

entries.clue: The oratorio one long expected (7)

blocks.note: Handel's 1741 choral work, the one every amateur choir sings at Christmas
in scripture, the promised deliverer whose coming has been awaited for centuries

annotation.surface: An oratorio that audiences have been waiting a very long time to hear.
annotation.walkthrough: Handel wrote the piece in three weeks and named it after the figure the second half describes, so the two definitions are one step apart rather than unrelated. A capital letter would have given the whole thing away.
annotation.definitionFit: Handel's oratorio carries the name, and in Jewish and Christian scripture the Messiah is the deliverer whose arrival has been promised for centuries.

entries.clue: Rearranged Mary, Luke and Jacob’s headgear (8)

indicatorNotes.Rearranged: Rearranging something puts its parts in a new order, and the parts here are the letters of the two names.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

annotation.surface: Three biblical names, the last of them wearing a hat.
annotation.walkthrough: Jacob is doing the job of a nationality: the skullcap is Jewish, and the name says so without saying it. Mary and Luke are fodder only, though they look like more of the same list.
annotation.definitionFit: A yarmulke is the skullcap Jewish men wear, and Jacob — the patriarch renamed Israel — stands in for the Jewish wearer.

entries.clue: Severe critic of players, one fierce creature (10)

blocks.note: the cast is the company of players in a production
i = one, the Roman numeral
gator is the American short form of alligator

annotation.surface: A harsh reviewer of a stage company, and one savage animal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Players' is the theatre's word here rather than sport's, and 'of' is joinery. Gator is the Americanism the crossword reaches for whenever a fierce creature has to be short.
annotation.definitionFit: To castigate is to rebuke somebody severely, so a castigator is precisely the person who hands out that kind of criticism.

entries.clue: Canal bridge to rail off (6)

indicatorNotes.off: Milk that has gone off has turned, and letters that turn come out in a different order from the one they were given in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters

annotation.surface: A bridge over a canal being fenced off.
annotation.walkthrough: The Rialto is the marble arch over Venice's Grand Canal. The fodder sits so quietly in the sentence that 'off' reads as part of the fencing job rather than an instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: The Rialto is the stone bridge crossing the Grand Canal in Venice, the city's oldest and best known canal crossing.

entries.clue: Hallo – is energy briefly produced from this? (3,5)

annotation.definition: Hallo – is energy briefly produced from this?

indicatorNotes.produced from: Something produced from a set of materials is made out of them in a new shape, so the letters are rebuilt in another order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
e = energy, the symbol in E=mc², which is the short form 'briefly' asks for

annotation.surface: Somebody greeting you and asking whether the lump of rock in their hand can be burned for power.
annotation.walkthrough: A greeting is unlikely fodder, which is what makes the first three words look like scene-setting. Read straight, the whole sentence is a fair question to ask about the answer, so definition and anagram occupy the same words.
annotation.definitionFit: Oil shale is the rock that oil and gas are cooked out of, so the whole clue is a reasonable question to ask while holding a piece of it.

entries.clue: Notice an attempt to restrict one, so scored slowly (6)

indicatorNotes.to restrict: To restrict something is to hem it in on both sides, so the letter named goes inside the word in front of it.

blocks.note: ad = advertisement, the notice in a newspaper
a is the other form of the same indefinite article
a go is an attempt, as in having a go at something
i = one, the Roman numeral

annotation.surface: Noticing an effort to keep a single person in check.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Notice' is the verb the sentence wants and the two-letter noun the wordplay wants. 'So scored' is joinery with a musical smell to it, pointing at the word a composer writes above the stave.
annotation.definitionFit: Adagio is the Italian tempo mark a composer writes to say a passage is to be played slowly.

entries.clue: Boy’s favourite drug (4)

blocks.note: your pet subject is your favourite one
e = ecstasy, the tablet

annotation.surface: A lad's drug of choice.
annotation.walkthrough: The possessive is doing the work of 'is': a boy is this. E for ecstasy is worth filing away, since it is the crossword's standard drug.
annotation.definitionFit: Pete is the everyday short form of Peter, so 'boy' names it the way crosswords name any common first name.

entries.clue: Copper and iron for example in mass with the others in depots (4,6)

indicatorNotes.in depots: Goods put in a depot are put inside it, so the letters named go within the word for those buildings.

blocks.note: a base is a depot, the store an army keeps its supplies in
m = mass, the physicist's letter for it
et al is the Latin for 'and the others', used after the first name in a list

annotation.surface: Metals kept in bulk alongside everything else in the stores.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The others' is Latin waiting to happen — a reading list writes it et al. 'Mass' looks like a quantity of stuff and hands over the physicist's single letter instead.
annotation.definitionFit: Base metals are the cheap corrodible ones — copper, iron, lead — as against gold and the other noble metals, so the two named are examples.

entries.clue: Son lazed about and moved furtively (6)

blocks.note: s = son, as written in a family tree
to idle is to laze about doing nothing much

annotation.surface: A son who loafed around all day and then slipped off quietly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' belongs to the loafing rather than to any turning of letters: idled about is one ordinary phrase. The single letter for son is one to learn, since the crossword uses it constantly.
annotation.definitionFit: To sidle is to move sideways and quietly so as not to be noticed, which is moving furtively.

entries.clue: Docker who has lost a lot of weight? (10)

annotation.definition2: who has lost a lot of weight?

blocks.note: the straight sense: a man whose trade is working the craft that carry cargo between ship and quay

blocks.clueFragment: who has lost a lot of weight?
blocks.note: the same ten letters split after the seventh: a fellow who weighs less than he did

annotation.surface: A dockworker who has slimmed down a great deal.
annotation.walkthrough: A lighter is a flat-bottomed barge used to unload ships out in the river, and the man who works one takes his job title straight from it. The second half wants those letters read as two ordinary words instead.
annotation.definitionFit: He crews a lighter, the barge ferrying cargo between ship and quay; re-split as two words the same letters describe a man who now weighs less.

entries.clue: Austins age, Rolls get replaced (8)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition names the model by its maker: every Allegro was an Austin, though plenty of Austins were something else.

indicatorNotes.get replaced: When things get replaced they are swapped one for another, and letters swapped about end up in a new order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

annotation.surface: A garage where the Austins are getting on and the Rolls-Royces are being swapped for new ones.
annotation.walkthrough: The Austin Allegro was British Leyland's much-mocked family car of the 1970s, sold for a while with a square steering wheel. 'Rolls' looks like the other half of a showroom and is fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: The Allegro was a model built and badged by Austin, so the maker's name stands in for the cars by example.

entries.clue: Art without tears? (7)

blocks.note: the straight half: a craft practised as an art form, Japanese in origin
two readings at once — the old phrase for a painless lesson, and paper that is folded and never ripped

annotation.surface: An art form you can pick up without any pain.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Without tears' is the schoolbook promise of a painless lesson, as in Rattigan's French Without Tears. The other reading needs the other pronunciation, and turns on paper being folded rather than torn.
annotation.definitionFit: Origami is the Japanese art of folding paper into shapes, and folding alone does all of it — nothing is ever torn.

entries.clue: Tiny thing, skin blemish? Bad clue (8)

indicatorNotes.Bad: A bad copy of something has its parts out of true, so the letters that follow are written in the wrong order.

blocks.note: a mole is the small dark spot on the skin
the four letters of CLUE in a new order

annotation.surface: A grumble about a speck, a blotch on the skin and a badly written clue.
annotation.walkthrough: The setter is running himself down: the last two words call one of his own clues bad, and that self-criticism is where the anagram lives. 'Tiny thing' is deliberately loose about how tiny.
annotation.definitionFit: A molecule is the smallest unit of a substance that still keeps its chemical identity, and the word is used loosely of anything minute.

entries.clue: Scatter finest roses (except white, initially) (7)

indicatorNotes.initially: Taking words initially means taking only the letter each one starts with, in the order they are written.

blocks.note: the finest of anything is the best of it
the opening letters of ROSES, EXCEPT and WHITE

annotation.surface: Somebody told to spread the best roses about, leaving the white ones out of it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Except' looks like an instruction to leave something out, and instead surrenders its own first letter alongside the words on either side of it. Bestrew is an old literary verb, common in Shakespeare.
annotation.definitionFit: To bestrew a place is to scatter things all over it, the strewing verb with an old intensifying prefix on the front.

entries.clue: Former soldier, American, shielding deserter as a favour (2,6)

indicatorNotes.shielding: To shield somebody is to put yourself around them, so the word named next sits inside the letters before it.

blocks.note: your ex is your former partner
a GI is an enlisted American soldier, from 'government issue'
a rat is one who deserts his own side
a = American, the usual abbreviation

annotation.surface: An ex-serviceman and an American hiding a man who ran away, and doing it as a kindness.
annotation.walkthrough: 'American' has its own small job to do after the soldier has already arrived from America, which is the easiest step to lose. An ex gratia payment admits no liability at all.
annotation.definitionFit: An ex gratia payment is made out of goodwill rather than any legal duty, which is exactly handing it over as a favour.

entries.clue: River creature’s back consisting of thin plates (7)

indicatorNotes.back: In a down clue back means up the grid, so the letters assembled so far are read from the end to the start.

blocks.note: r = river, as printed on any map
a creature is an animal

annotation.surface: The back of some animal in a river.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Creature's back' looks like an order to take the last letter of the word, and it is the whole assembly that turns instead. Laminar flow is the engineer's name for fluid moving in smooth parallel layers.
annotation.definitionFit: Laminar means made up of laminae — thin sheets or plates lying one on top of another.

entries.clue: Wrap everything before I jog back (8)

indicatorNotes.before: What comes before a thing is written in front of it, so the first chunk is set down ahead of the letter that follows.
indicatorNotes.back: Something told to go back is read the other way round, so the whole run of letters is turned end for end.

blocks.note: everything is all of it
the speaker, written as the single letter the clue gives
to trot is to jog along at a steady pace

annotation.surface: Somebody asking you to package everything up before they jog home.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes the first word a verb, and the answer is the flatbread you roll a filling into. Everything after that first word is written backwards, the letter for the speaker included.
annotation.definitionFit: A wrap is a tortilla rolled round a filling, so the sandwich shop uses the two words for the same lunch.

entries.clue: Old French tax in force – tire of it regularly (6)

indicatorNotes.regularly: Letters taken regularly are taken at a steady interval, here every second one right across the phrase.

blocks.note: every second letter of fOrCe TiRe Of It

annotation.surface: A levy still in force that you gradually grow tired of.
annotation.walkthrough: The even letters run straight through the dash and the word breaks, which is what makes the pick hard to see. An octroi was the duty a French town charged on goods carried in through its gates.
annotation.definitionFit: The octroi was the toll levied at the gates of a French town on food and goods brought in, abolished in the twentieth century.

entries.clue: Go without, to feed my pride? (6)

annotation.definitionNote: Strictly the verb for doing without is forgo; dictionaries record this longer spelling as an accepted variant of it, and that is the one the grid wants.

blocks.note: what you feed a thing is given for it, so the phrase comes down to 'for'
the ego is the self, and pride in oneself is what it consists of

annotation.surface: Going without something in order to keep my own self-regard well fed.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark is apologising for the definition: strictly it is forgo that means to do without, while the spelling here means to go before. Ego is Latin for 'I', which is why 'my pride' shrinks to three letters.
annotation.definitionFit: To forgo something is to go without it, and this spelling has been accepted as a variant of that verb for centuries.

entries.clue: Holiday by car (6)

blocks.note: the Spanish word for a festival day, taken into English for any carnival
Ford's small hatchback, on British driveways since 1976

annotation.surface: A holiday taken by car.
annotation.walkthrough: 'By' looks like the means of travel and is only joinery. The Ford was Britain's best-selling car for most of forty years, which is what makes a bare 'car' fair for it.
annotation.definitionFit: A fiesta is a Spanish religious festival or public holiday, and Ford has sold a small family car under the same name since 1976.

entries.clue: Pretty drawing (10)

blocks.note: good-looking, the everyday sense of the word
pulling things towards itself, the way a magnet does

annotation.surface: A nice sketch.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drawing' is the magnet's verb rather than the artist's, and the two words sit side by side with nothing joining them. Both definitions are adjectives, though the second is dressed as a participle.
annotation.definitionFit: Something attractive is pretty to look at, and the same word describes anything that draws people or objects towards it.

entries.clue: Provision of food cut down a bit for pig (4)

indicatorNotes.cut down a bit: Cutting a bit off a thing takes its tail end away, so the last letter goes.

blocks.note: food supplied along with your lodging, as in 'bed and ―' at a guest house, with the last letter then dropping

annotation.surface: Rations being trimmed to feed a pig.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Board' for food is the word inside 'full board' and 'bed and board', lodgings that come with meals. The surface hides the cut inside a sentence about a farm animal's dinner.
annotation.definitionFit: A boar is the male pig, wild or domestic, so the general word names it by its class.

entries.clue: I’m shivering in second class, getting basic education (4)

annotation.definitionNote: The answer is a noise rather than a word, so the definition has to be the whole sentence a shivering person is saying by making it.

blocks.note: a B is a second-class grade or mark
the three Rs — reading, writing and arithmetic — is the old name for a basic schooling

annotation.surface: Freezing in a second-class carriage while getting an elementary education.
annotation.walkthrough: The three Rs are reading, writing and arithmetic, named so as to pretend all three begin with the same letter. 'Second class' is the schoolroom's mark here, not the railway's cheap seat.
annotation.definitionFit: Brrr is the written form of the noise a shivering person makes, so it says the words aloud rather than describing them.

entries.clue: Extra reason cricket was held up? (2,4)

blocks.note: in cricket's scorebook, a run credited to the side rather than to the batter
the whimsical half: with nothing to bowl, nobody can start the game

annotation.surface: The reason a cricket match was delayed.
annotation.walkthrough: Cricket calls runs that come off no bat 'extras', and an illegal delivery hands the batting side one of them. The second half is the joke, reading the answer as two ordinary words about missing kit.
annotation.definitionFit: A no-ball is an unlawful delivery that gives the batting side a penalty run, and such runs are exactly what cricket calls extras.

entries.clue: Foolishly rides to a distant rock (8)

indicatorNotes.Foolishly: Doing something foolishly is doing it wrong, and letters written down wrong come out in the wrong order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

annotation.surface: Somebody riding recklessly out to a far-off crag.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Distant rock' is vague on purpose: it could be a sea stack or a moon, and only the crossing letters settle it. Everything between the first word and the definition is fodder, little words included.
annotation.definitionFit: An asteroid is one of the rocky bodies orbiting the sun mostly between Mars and Jupiter, a long way off and made of rock.
